native_result.query: In which years were individuals with a criminal record found to have significantly lower wealth compared to those without?
native_result.HypoA: In 1985, 1990, and 1996, individuals with a criminal record have significantly lower wealth compared to those without.
native_result.HypoB: In all three observed years - 1985, 1990 and 1996 - respondents with a criminal record (ever_jailed = 1, jailed between 1985 and 1994; n = 289) held significantly lower composite wealth than those never jailed (n = 11,724), and the gap widened over time. In 1985 mean wealth was $7,929 vs $25,086 (difference -$17,157; 95% CI -20,603 to -13,711; bootstrap -20,364 to -13,621; one-sided Welch p = 3.2e-21, Holm-adjusted 9.5e-21; Mann-Whitney p = 8.0e-11; Cliff's delta = -0.22; medians $720 vs $3,600); in 1990 $16,350 vs $73,948 (-$57,598; CI -69,428 to -45,768; p = 7.8e-20, Holm 7.8e-20; MWU 3.9e-35; delta = -0.42; medians $0 vs $10,500); in 1996 $20,383 vs $105,447 (-$85,063; CI -102,274 to -67,853; p = 3.6e-20, Holm 7.3e-20; MWU 4.6e-26; delta = -0.35; medians $0 vs $8,500). The pattern survives adjustment for sex and race (asinh-wealth beta = -0.49, -1.45, -1.63; all p <= 1.7e-06), median regression (-$1,100, -$3,800, -$6,000), permutation tests, and every sensitivity variant (zeros treated as missing, wealth>0 only, deduplicated rows, winsorized, trimmed means); the wealth ratio fell from 0.32 to 0.22 to 0.19, and both the share with wealth <= 0 (45/57/63% vs 32/29/40%) and mean wealth among positive-wealth respondents (difference -$22k, -$67k, -$121k) contributed. The association is descriptive, not causal: the exposure window is 1985-1994, so the 1985 difference reflects a pre-existing wealth gap / selection into incarceration rather than a consequence of it, and the unweighted data (1,899 exact duplicate rows; wealth zeros that may include survey nonresponse) are not representative of the U.S. population.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) QC of data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 x 6, no missing values, race label 'hipanic' kept, ever_jailed 289 vs 11,724, 1,899 exact duplicate rows noted). 2) Main sample = full file; exposure = ever_jailed only, no derived features. 3) Primary per-year contrasts on raw dollars (1985, 1990, 1996): one-sided Welch t-test (H1: jailed < never) and one-sided Mann-Whitney U, with Holm correction across the 3 years within each test family at alpha = 0.05; two-sided p-values and 95% t CIs reported alongside; 10,000-replicate percentile bootstrap CIs for differences in means and medians; 10,000-swap permutation test as a distribution-free check. 4) Effect sizes: Cliff's delta on raw wealth, Hedges g on asinh(wealth/1000). 5) Confirmatory regressions: OLS asinh(wealth/1000) ~ ever_jailed + C(sex) + C(race) with HC3 SEs (unadjusted coefficient shown in the same table) and median (quantile) regression with the same covariates. 6) Decision rule: a year counts as robust if direction agrees in all analyses (mean difference, median difference, adjusted asinh beta, median-regression beta, Cliff's delta) AND Holm-adjusted p < 0.05 in both primary families. 7) Decomposition of the gap into the extensive margin (share with wealth <= 0; chi-square and logistic regression adjusted for sex+race) and the intensive margin E[wealth | wealth > 0] with bootstrap CI, showing the finding is not produced by zero-filled attrition. 8) Sensitivity: A main (zeros+duplicates kept), B zeros as missing, C wealth>0 only, D exact duplicate rows dropped, E winsorized at 1st/99th percentile, plus Yuen-Welch 10%-trimmed means. 9) Exploratory sex x race appendix with cell sizes (n_jailed 9-16 in female cells) flagged as low power and excluded from the answer wording. 10) Outputs: results_table_primary.csv, results_table_sensitivity.csv, results_table_appendix_sexrace.csv, results_summary.md.

sub_hypo.text: In 1985, 1990, and 1996, individuals with a criminal record have significantly lower wealth compared to those without.
sub_hypo.context: Participants in the National Longitudinal Study of Youth's 1979 cohort, with wealth measured in 1985, 1990, and 1996.
sub_hypo.relations: Individuals with a criminal record, operationalized as having been jailed between 1985 and 1994 (ever_jailed = 1), have significantly lower composite wealth in each of 1985, 1990, and 1996 than those without (ever_jailed = 0).

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: In 1985, 1990, and 1996, individuals with a criminal record have significantly lower wealth compared to those without.

sub_hypo.text: Respondents jailed between 1985 and 1994 had significantly lower composite wealth in 1985, 1990, and 1996 than respondents never jailed, and the absolute wealth gap widened over time.
sub_hypo.context: Full unweighted National Longitudinal Study of Youth 1979 cohort dataset: 12,013 rows, including 289 ever-jailed and 11,724 never-jailed respondents. Observed wealth years are 1985, 1990, and 1996. The main analysis retains zeros and 1,899 exact duplicate rows; zeros may include survey nonresponse. Findings are descriptive, not causal or representative of the U.S. population. The 1985 gap reflects pre-existing differences or selection into incarceration, not a consequence of incarceration during the 1985–1994 exposure window.
sub_hypo.relations: Ever-jailed versus never-jailed mean wealth was $7,929 versus $25,086 in 1985, $16,350 versus $73,948 in 1990, and $20,383 versus $105,447 in 1996; reported differences were -$17,157, -$57,598, and -$85,063. Wealth ratios declined from 0.32 to 0.22 to 0.19. Medians were $720 versus $3,600, $0 versus $10,500, and $0 versus $8,500. Both one-sided Welch and Mann–Whitney tests were significant after Holm correction across years at alpha = 0.05, with Cliff's delta of -0.22, -0.42, and -0.35.

sub_hypo.text: The negative association between incarceration status and wealth in all three years persists after adjustment for sex and race and across distribution-free checks and sensitivity analyses.
sub_hypo.context: Same NLSY 1979 cohort sample and 1985, 1990, and 1996 wealth observations. Adjusted analyses use sex and race as covariates. Sensitivity analyses treat zeros as missing, restrict wealth to positive values, remove exact duplicate rows, winsorize at the 1st and 99th percentiles, or use 10%-trimmed means. Associations remain descriptive rather than causal.
sub_hypo.relations: Sex- and race-adjusted OLS coefficients for ever_jailed on asinh(wealth/1000) were -0.49, -1.45, and -1.63 in chronological order, all with p <= 1.7e-06. Adjusted median-regression coefficients were -$1,100, -$3,800, and -$6,000. Negative directions agree across mean and median differences, adjusted regressions, and Cliff's delta; permutation tests and every specified sensitivity variant support the pattern.

sub_hypo.text: Both a higher share of respondents with nonpositive wealth and lower mean wealth among positive-wealth respondents contribute to the wealth disadvantage of ever-jailed respondents.
sub_hypo.context: Same NLSY 1979 cohort dataset, comparing ever-jailed and never-jailed respondents in 1985, 1990, and 1996. The extensive margin uses wealth <= 0; the intensive margin restricts each year's comparison to wealth > 0. Extensive-margin analyses include logistic regression adjusted for sex and race.
sub_hypo.relations: Shares with wealth <= 0 were 45%, 57%, and 63% among ever-jailed respondents versus 32%, 29%, and 40% among never-jailed respondents in 1985, 1990, and 1996. Among respondents with positive wealth, ever-jailed minus never-jailed mean differences were approximately -$22,000, -$67,000, and -$121,000. Both margins contribute to the gap, so it is not produced solely by zero-filled attrition.
